title: Ashtpadi 17, salok: true in the beginning
hookLine: aad sach: the same salok as Japji's opening returns (Sukhmani 17)

lines: A NEW SONG, THEN AN OLD ONE.
THE FIRST PAGE OF THE GURU.
cards: You're halfway through a long, new song, and suddenly the band plays the opening bars of one you've known since childhood. It stops you. You know where you are.
Something like that happens at the seventeenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani.

After sixteen ashtpadis of Guru Arjan's own words, the salok is a line Sikhs know from the very first page of the Guru Granth Sahib: the line right after the Mool Mantar, which opens Japji Sahib every morning.
Words Sikhs know as Guru Nanak's, coming back inside Guru Arjan's hymn.

teach.b: Here it is in Punjabi first, the way it's recited every morning. Aad sach, jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach, Nanak, hosee bhee sach.
In paraphrase: true in the beginning, true through the ages. True now, Nanak, and true it will be. Sach is truth, and in Gurbani it means more than not lying.
Sach is what's real, what lasts, what holds. The line walks it through every kind of time. Aad: the beginning, before anything began.
Jugaad: through the ages, the long eras of the world. Hai bhee: is, right now. Hosee bhee: will be, after everything we know is gone.
Four steps, and the truth is the same at every one. Why would Guru Arjan bring it back here? Sukhmani doesn't say, and the sources don't record his reason, so we can only notice what it does.
It ties the hymn to the root of the scripture: Sukhmani by the fifth Guru, Japji by the first.

Sikhs hear in it one teaching passed from Guru to Guru, like one flame lit from another; they describe the Gurus that way, ten bodies, one light. It also helps anyone reciting Sukhmani, a long recitation.
Deep in the middle, when attention fades, here is a line the tongue already knows.
You come home to it. And it sets up what follows: the seventeenth ashtpadi is about truth, and it starts by saying truth doesn't change with the times.

how: Sikhs recite aad sach, jugaad sach as the salok after the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji Sahib each morning, and meet the same salok again at the opening of Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi.

o: truth: what's real, what lasts, what holds
a polite word for a promise or a vow
honesty, simply not telling any lies

games.q: the salok of ashtpadi 17 — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're deep in Sukhmani, a long recitation, and your attention is fading. what greets you at the seventeenth ashtpadi?
o: the salok Sikhs know from Japji's first page.
games.why: aad sach, jugaad sach: Guru Nanak's line returns inside Guru Arjan's hymn, one light passed from Guru to Guru.

practice: Say it once, slowly: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, hosee bhee sach, or in English, true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, true to come.
Then let it settle, and bring to mind one thing in your life that was true at the start and is still true now. Rest there.

wordCard.voice: Sach, truth, what's real and lasts. The salok is Japji's: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, hosee bhee sach, true in the beginning, through the ages, now, and to come.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sach, truth, the real, what lasts.

carryVoice: Your line: true then, true now. Moods and news shift, and the line doesn't. Day five hundred two, done.
